analysis.one_liner: Mandates federal reliability standards for the electricity grid, efficiency savings targets, and net metering for rooftop solar.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create enforceable federal rules to keep the electric grid from failing, require utilities to cut electricity waste and peak demand every year, help low-income households pay energy bills through a new trust fund, and force utilities to buy back excess power from homes and businesses with rooftop solar or other on-site generation. It also creates an independent board to investigate major blackouts and a National Academy of Sciences study of grid vulnerabilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary electricity customers get more reliable power, lower bills from mandatory efficiency savings, and the right to install rooftop solar and get credited for excess power. Low-income households get matching federal funds for energy assistance. Emergency services like police, fire, and hospitals get renewable backup power. Grid workers get a model safety code.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electricity customers, low-income households, rooftop solar owners

how_it_helps.text: Grants the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authority to approve and enforce mandatory reliability standards on all bulk power system users, owners, and operators, with penalties for violations [S2] [S3].

Requires electric retail suppliers to achieve verified reductions in peak demand and total electricity use, reaching 10% demand reduction by 2013, with refunds to customers if utilities fall short [S2] [S3].

Requires every electric utility to offer net metering to residential customers up to 25 kilowatts and commercial customers up to 1,000 kilowatts using renewable sources, with credit for excess generation and no extra standby charges [S2] [S3].

Creates a System Benefits Trust Fund, funded by a charge on electricity carried over the wires, to match state spending on energy conservation, renewable energy, and low-income home energy assistance [S2] [S3].

Establishes an independent Electricity Outage Investigation Board to determine the causes of major bulk-power system failures and recommend preventive actions, and directs a National Academy of Sciences study of grid reliability and vulnerability including sabotage [S2] [S3].

Authorizes $10 billion in federal loan guarantees for projects enhancing grid reliability, security, and efficiency, prioritizing environmentally beneficial approaches, and a $30 million annual demonstration program for renewable backup power at emergency facilities [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities and transmission operators pay penalties for reliability violations, absorb the cost of efficiency programs, and can no longer charge special fees to customers who generate their own power. All customers pay a small wires charge of up to 0.1 cents per kilowatt-hour into the trust fund. Taxpayers cover loan guarantee and demonstration program costs. Traditional utilities lose some revenue as customers reduce consumption and generate their own electricity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Electric utilities and all electricity customers

drawbacks.text: The wires charge funding the trust fund would raise costs for all electricity customers, including those who cannot reduce their own usage [S3].

Mandatory efficiency targets could force utilities to raise rates to fund demand-reduction programs, and the bill requires spending 125% of any shortfall through competitive bidding, a costly remedy if targets prove unachievable [S3].

Net metering requirements shift some grid maintenance costs to other customers when owners of on-site generation pay no standby or capacity charges, since they still rely on the grid for backup power [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit — preventing large-scale blackouts through enforceable standards — addresses a real public vulnerability, and the efficiency targets would likely save customers more than the small wires charge costs. The net metering cost shift and the aggressive 10% efficiency mandate are the strongest objections, but they are modest against the reliability and consumer benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it sat until Congress ended in January 2005 with no committee action, hearing, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeffords introduced the bill on October 17, 2003, for himself, Sen. Kennedy, and Sen. Cantwell, days after the August 2003 blackout that affected 50 million people [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on October 17, 2003 [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — was ever recorded; the Congress ended January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities and transmission operators are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory reliability penalties, efficiency mandates with customer refunds for shortfalls, and an end to special charges on customers who generate their own power. Ordinary customers did not get the reliability standards, efficiency savings, or net metering rights the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Electric utilities, which avoided mandates and penalties

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks [S1] [S5].

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was by an Independent (who caucused with Democrats) plus two Democrats, with no committee action ever taken, so no vote reveals the partisan split.

industries.note: They would face enforceable reliability standards with penalties, mandatory efficiency programs with customer refunds for shortfalls, and a wires charge, while losing revenue to efficiency and customer self-generation. Reliability standards also protect them from costly blackouts, so their interest in that piece runs with the public's, but they opposed the mandatory savings targets and net metering.

industries.industry: Rooftop solar and distributed renewable energy installers
industries.note: Mandatory net metering, no standby charges, and guaranteed interconnection would expand the market for on-site renewable generation and its installation industry.

industries.industry: Grid technology and efficiency equipment makers
industries.note: Loan guarantees and the efficiency mandate would drive demand for high-efficiency transmission controls, storage, combined heat and power, and energy efficiency systems.
